source_text: Si veritatem Apostoli verbis vindicas nec eum impudenter putas fuisse mentitum, doce, quemadmodum de naturali peccato dicenti haec sententia non incutiat publicae falsitatis pudorem. Nam si esset originale peccatum, quod omnem omnino naturam hominum ad ius diaboli faceret pertinere, qui erat locus ad aequiparandum partium numerum, eorum videlicet qui salvantur, et illorum qui intereunt? In Evangelio Dominus, cum beatorum ostenderet raritatem: Quam arta et angusta - inquit - via, quae ducit ad vitam, et pauci sunt, qui inveniunt eam! Quam lata et spatiosa via, quae ducit ad perditionem, et multi sunt, qui intrant per eam! [n331]
pass_a_gloss: If you vindicate truth for the Apostle's words and do not shamelessly think that he lied, teach how this sentence does not strike a shame of public falsehood upon one speaking about a natural sin. For if there were an original sin, which would make every nature of human beings altogether belong to the devil's right, what place was there toward equalizing the number of the parts, namely of those who are saved and of those who perish? In the Gospel the Lord, when he was showing the rarity of the blessed: How narrow and strait, he says, the way which leads unto life, and few are who find it! How broad and spacious the way which leads unto perdition, and many are who enter through it!

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin

pass_b_english: If you uphold the truth of the apostle’s words and do not think he lied shamelessly, explain how this statement would not bring on him the disgrace of public falsehood if he were speaking about natural sin. If original sin existed, making absolutely all human nature belong to the devil’s jurisdiction, where would there be room even to make the numbers on the two sides equal—those saved and those perishing? In the Gospel, when the Lord showed how few are blessed, he said: ‘How narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it! How broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it!’ (Matthew 7:13–14).

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
